dataset.name: BrainActive P3 High Ability Verbal Extension
dataset.disclaimer: Original reasoning-practice items inspired by the BrainActive verbal-reasoning research (MOE 2026 HAL context, GEP General Ability verbal archetypes, CogAT, UK 11+ VR). Not affiliated with or predictive of any MOE or GEP assessment. Not a mock exam. Not English tuition.
dataset.design: v0.5 is a RESEARCH-DERIVED VERBAL EXTENSION. 10 questions authored strictly from brainactive_verbal_pilot_plan.md (items A1-G1) to demonstrate the Verbal hierarchy (VR1-VR7). Difficulty rises via rule discovery, relation discovery and constraint count - NOT harder words. A2 (set/category analogy) and C1/C2/D1 (codes/word transformation) require discovering the operating rule, not mechanical application. v0.4.1 (50 Qs) is left untouched as the experimental baseline.
dataset.gates: No DB, no renderer, no production app code, no merge into v0.4.1. Extension file only.

questions.question: Leaf is to tree as page is to ___?
questions.explanation: Relation: a single part that, together with many others, makes up the whole. A leaf is one part of a tree; a page is one part of a book. (Paper is made from trees; word is what is printed on a page; cover is one part of a book but not the 'many parts make the whole' part.)
questions.reasoning: Finding a part-whole relation and applying it to a new pair.

provenance.source_inspiration: v0.5 verbal extension, pilot plan A1 (research-derived). Builds VR1 beyond 0037/0013.

questions.question: Cup, plate, bowl : rose, tulip, sunflower : apple, banana, ___?
questions.explanation: The relation is NOT a word pair. Each group is a set of three things in the same category: Group 1 = things you eat from (dishes); Group 2 = flowers; Group 3 = fruits. The missing member of the fruit set is orange. (Carrot is a vegetable, not a fruit; leaf and tree are not fruits.)
questions.reasoning: Discovering that the relation is category-to-category (set correspondence), then completing the last set.

provenance.source_inspiration: v0.5 verbal extension, pilot plan A2 (research-derived). GEP GA set-analogy archetype (S3), P3-accessible.

questions.question: Which word is the odd one out?  A red  B blue  C green  D circle
questions.explanation: Red, blue and green are colours. Circle is a shape, so it does not belong to the colour group.
questions.reasoning: Grouping words by meaning (semantic category), not by sound or look.

provenance.source_inspiration: v0.5 verbal extension, pilot plan B1 (research-derived).

questions.question: Which does NOT belong?  A clock  B watch  C timer  D ruler
questions.explanation: Clock, watch and timer are all things that tell or measure TIME. A ruler measures LENGTH, not time, so it is the odd one out. The grouping is by function, not by how the objects look.
questions.reasoning: Finding a non-obvious shared property (function) and rejecting a surface-feature grouping.

provenance.source_inspiration: v0.5 verbal extension, pilot plan B2 (research-derived).

questions.question: In a code, a letter is worth the SQUARE of its place in the alphabet (A=1, B=4, C=9, D=16 ...). Which letter is worth 25?
questions.explanation: The values are squares: 1, 4, 9, 16 ... so 25 = 5 squared. E is the 5th letter of the alphabet, therefore E = 25. (Y is the 25th letter - a near-miss if you match the number to the letter directly; F would be 6; S would be 19.)
questions.reasoning: Discovering the square rule from the examples, then mapping a square root back to a letter position.

provenance.source_inspiration: v0.5 verbal extension, pilot plan C1 (research-derived). GEP letter-number code (S4).

questions.question: In a code, DOG becomes GLJ and CAT becomes FDW. The rule is: move the 1st letter forward 3, the 2nd letter back 3, the 3rd letter forward 3, and keep alternating. What does PIG become?
questions.explanation: Apply the alternating rule to PIG: P forward 3 = S; I back 3 = F; G forward 3 = J. So PIG becomes SFJ. (SLJ is if every letter moved forward 3; SFD is if the last letter also moved back; MFJ is if the first moved back.)
questions.reasoning: Inferring an alternating +/- shift rule from two examples, then applying it to a new word.

provenance.source_inspiration: v0.5 verbal extension, pilot plan C2 (research-derived).

questions.question: In a code, TRAIN becomes RAINT and PLANT becomes LANTP. The rule moves the FIRST letter to the END. What does HOUSE become?
questions.explanation: Move the first letter H to the end of HOUSE and you get OUSEH. (USEHO moves the LAST letter to the front; EHOSU reverses the word; HOUSE is unchanged.)
questions.reasoning: Discovering a transformation rule (first letter to end) from two examples, then applying it.

provenance.source_inspiration: v0.5 verbal extension, pilot plan D1 (research-derived). Fills VR4 gap noted in framework.

questions.question: A letter pattern goes: B, D, G, K, ___. The gap grows by 1 each step (B to D is +2, D to G is +3, G to K is +4). What comes next?
questions.explanation: The next gap is +5. K is the 11th letter, so 11 + 5 = 16 = P. (O would be +4 again; Q would be +6; N would be +3.)
questions.reasoning: Finding a changing rule (gap increases by 1) and extending the pattern.

provenance.source_inspiration: v0.5 verbal extension, pilot plan E1 (research-derived). UK GL letter-series archetype (S11/S13).

questions.question: Three boxes are red, blue and green. Each holds one thing: a book, a ball or a coin. (1) The blue box holds the book. (2) The red box does not hold the ball. (3) The green box does not hold the coin. What does the green box hold?
questions.explanation: Blue = book, so red and green share ball and coin. Red does NOT hold the ball, so red = coin. That leaves green = ball. Clue (3) is the consistency check: green does not hold the coin - true, so the assignment holds.
questions.reasoning: Combining three constraints to fix a unique assignment (deduction, not guess).

provenance.source_inspiration: v0.5 verbal extension, pilot plan F1 (research-derived).

questions.question: The ground was wet, so we took our ___.
questions.explanation: Wet ground means rain, so an umbrella keeps you dry - it fits the cause (wet) and the effect (take ...). A shoe is worn anyway; a book and an apple do not fit the situation.
questions.reasoning: Using sentence context (cause and effect) to pick the fitting word.

provenance.source_inspiration: v0.5 verbal extension, pilot plan G1 (research-derived). Capped B-type (S6/S9).
